dcterms:title: Soundwagon disc phonograph
dcterms:description:
Contextual Associations
The Soundwagon phonograph is an electro-acoustic idiophone stylusphone designed and manufactured in Japan but distributed and sold widely throughout the world. Shaped like a Volkswagen campervan (this likeness is officially licensed by Volkswagen), this Soundwagon can be used only to play 33-1/3rpm micro-groove disc records. It is a monaural phonograph (stereo records can be played by it, but as though they are monaural records). Although the word “toy” is sometimes used in writings about this phonograph, the manufacturer (Stokyo Co., Ltd.) warns the purchaser of this phonograph that it is not a toy and that it is “not recommended for children” (bottom of packaging box). The manufacturer pitches the phonograph as “a unique record player unlike anything seen before. While an ordinary phonograph player rotates the vinyl, the ‘Soundwagon’ propels itself around the record, playing music from it’s [sic] own built in Speaker! Whether for record playing, amusement, vinyl digging at garage sales or record stores, the ‘Soundwagon’ is your perfect mobile record player” (bottom of packaging box). It is, indeed, mobile, for it runs on a single 9-volt battery rather than having to be plugged into a wall socket. 
Description
Colored plastic is used for the phonograph casing: candy blue and white trim for the campervan body; black for its chassis and tires (which do not rotate). Access to the phonograph’s interior was not possible, so there can be no descriptions provided for the machine’s amplifier, loudspeaker, and other internal components. The stylus is rear-facing and the two electrical wires (one red, the other white) connecting the cartridge transducer to the player’s electrical power source and to its amplifier run nearly the length of the stylus carriage before they disappear into the interior of the phonograph (detail #1). A guide wheel, also part of the pivoting stylus/cartridge carriage, assists in keeping the gem-tipped stylus in the record groove, while the phonograph’s drive wheel, which propels the phonograph around the surface of the disc, is located inside the right-rear tire (detail #1, upper right corner). The on/off switch is in the form of a long antennae protruding from the left side of the phonograph’s body (gallery #1). In detail #5, the speaker grill, located on the roof of the camper, can be seen. The ‘Soundwagon’ is marketed in a cardboard box from which much of the information in this essay was taken (gallery #2).
Player - Instrument Interface and Sound Production
Place either a monaural or stereo 33-1/3rpm disc on a flat surface (such as a tabletop). If not already provided with a 9-volt battery, insert one through the van’s rear door (details #2 and #3). Release the stylus carriage from its storage hook (detail #4 shows the stylus carriage attached to the storage hook), rotate the power switch to its ‘on’ position, and place the Soundwagon on the record so that it moves counterclockwise around the disc it is playing (video clip). It has no controls for volume, tone, or speed. When the operator is finished listening to the contents of the phonogram, the phonograph is lifted off the record and the power switch is moved to its ‘off’ position.
Origins/History/Evolution
A prototype (not marketed) of the ‘Soundwago” called “Chorocco”, made by Sony, was displayed in 1976 in Japan. This novelty phonograph was first marketed in 1982 by Tamco as the “Soundwagon” and was eventually picked up by Stokyo (date unknown) which, later (the mid-2010s), re-designed and renamed it as the “Record Runner”. [The example of this phonograph in the Grinnell Collection is closest to the Tamco and earlier Stokyo designs of the Soundwagon.]

hyoshigi
dcterms:description:
Contextual Associations
The hyoshigi is a concussion idiophone of the Japanese people of Japan. It is a sound effects instrument used in the kabuki theatre of Japan to “signal performers and stage personnel and to indicate the opening and closing of the curtain.” (Motegi, p. 659). It is considered an instrument developed specifically for the kabuki theatre, but it is also found outside of this context where it is used by night watchmen, fire watchers, and candy salesmen (Malm, p.225; Marcuse, p.255).
Description
The hyoshigi is comprised of two identical solid rectangular blocks of an unknown variety of hardwood (gallery #1). One of the wider faces of each block is absolutely flat (detail #1), and it is these two faces that are concussed against one another. The opposite face of each block is slightly arched (detail #2). The end of each block is marked with a Japanese character, a different one at each end (see details #3 and #4)
Player - Instrument Interface and Sound Production
The hyoshigi is sounded in two ways in kabuki performances: 1) as concussion clappers used a) pre-performance to count down the minutes to the start of the performance, and b) to accompany the opening and closing of the stage curtain and to precede any dramatic poses struck by lead characters during a performance; and 2) as percussion sticks pounded against a non-sonorous wooden board resting on the stage to accentuate fight scenes. In both cases, one block is held in each hand by the stagehand known as the kyogen-kata (Malm, p.224).
Origins/History/Evolution
Other than Motegi stating that the hyoshigi is “an instrument developed specifically for the kabuki theatre,” our sources provide no other information about the origin of this instrument. It is possible that the instrument’s use outside of the kabuki theatre predated its introduction to that context, but no sources were found that state this.

dcterms:title: tsenatsil
dcterms:subject: 112.111  idiophone--strung rattle (sistrum); rattling objects are strung in rows on cord/s or wire/s the ends of which are attached to a frame
dcterms:description:
Contextual Associations
The tsenatsil is a shaken rattle idiophone of Ethiopia. It is used by priests in religious ceremonies of the Ethiopian Orthodox Christian church. Each part of the instrument carries symbolic meaning: “the handle represents God, the side arms represent the Old and New Testaments, three discs on the upper cross bar the Trinity, and two discs on the lower bar Jesus as Son of God and of Man” (Timkehet Teffera,p. 94). 
Description
The tsenatsil has two main parts (gallery #1): 1) a metal (brass?) horseshoe-shaped frame the sides of which are decorated with a geometric pattern (detail #1) and that includes the sliding sound-producing components of this instrument; and (2) the wood handle to which the frame is attached  The sound-producing component of this tsenatsil consists of five thin metal discs loosely strung on two wires (three discs on the top wire, two on the bottom one) the ends of which are anchored to the sides of the instrument’s metal frame (detail #2).
Player - Instrument Interface and Sound Production
According to Powne (1966 p.24), the tsenatsil is held in the left hand with the arm bent upward in front of the shoulder. It is gently shaken forward and back by the movement of the player’s wrist so that its discs bang against one another and against the walls of its frame. The rhythms produced on the tsenatsil follow musical rules and the chant texts that they accompany.
Origins/History/Evolution
Ethiopian legend attributes the use of the tsenatsil in the Ethiopian Orthodox Christian Church to St. Yared (lived c. 6th century CE), the purported creator of Ethiopian liturgical chant (Powne, p. 25).

dcterms:title: saxhorn baryton in C and B-flat (in circular form)
dcterms:subject: 423.232.22  aerophone – chromatic labrosone valve horn with intermediate bore and long air column (more than 2m)
dcterms:description:
Contextual Associations
The saxhorn baryton in C and B-flat is a medium conical bore end-blown labrosone aerophone produced in the second half of the 19th century in France and other European countries. This saxhorn baryton, produced by the French firm Gautrot Aîné (established by Pierre Louis Gautrot in 1845 and headed by him until his death in 1882), was possibly a variant form (circular, perhaps inspired by the shape of the French horn) of the saxhorn baryton patented by Adolphe Sax in 1845. From around 1869 to the early 1880s, Gautrot Breveté was the company’s standard line of instruments (mostly for military and non-professional municipal band players) with a cartouche featuring an anchor with the initials ‘G’ and ‘A’ (for ‘Gautrot Aîné’; see detail #1) at its sides. The ‘S. G. D. G.’ (‘Sans Garantie du Gouvernement’, ‘without government guarantee’) seen below ‘Gautrot Breveté‘ was a common disclaimer found on French-made musical instruments in the later-half of the 19th century (Martz). Given that the Gautrot Breveté line stamped with the anchor cartouche began in 1869 and that the name of the company changed in 1883 a year after Pierre Louis Gautrot’s death, this instrument was probably manufactured sometime between these two dates. Because no serial number can be found on the instrument, it is not possible to narrow down further its date of manufacture. It is very likely that this circular version of the saxhorn baryton was manufactured for only a short period of time and never really caught on. It is a testament to the inventiveness and business drive of 19th century instrument manufactures throughout Europe and the endless variations of valved brass instruments they designed, built, and marketed during that century, only a few of which have stood the test of time. Worldwide, the military band was being reinvented during the 19th century with the addition of valved chromatic brass instruments; instrument manufacturers sought lucrative contracts with militaries and exported whole sets of band instruments to such organizations around the world. This particular circular variant of the saxhorn baryton had found its way to Australia before becoming part of the Grinnell instrument collection, perhaps originally sold to a branch of the Australian military back in the 19th century. 
Description
This silver-coated brass instrument includes three tubing segments that fit into the end of its lead pipe: two tuning bits and one crook (detail #2). One is straight and looks as though it would accept a large French horn-like mouthpiece (detail #2, top); such a mouthpiece did not come with this instrument when acquired in 2026. The other two segments accept a deeper-cup mouthpiece (such a mouthpiece did come with this instrument, see detail #3): the straight one is a tuning bit (detail #2, middle); the other a crook with a single loop (detail #2, bottom). When the bit is used with the mouthpiece, the horn is pitched in C (8-foot) (gallery #1); when the crook is added to this combination (i.e., bit + crook + mouthpiece, as seen in gallery #2) the horn is tuned to a fundamental of B-flat (9-foot). After passing through a cylindrical tubing section that includes a tuning slide (the second of its two U-shaped bends), the instrument’s tubing enters the side of its first valve casing. Each of the instrument’s three Perinét valves, operated with the middle three fingers of the player’s right hand, has its spring mounted internally at the top of the piston (detail #4). After exiting the third valve’s casing, the instrument’s tubing begins to gradually increase in diameter as it coils twice in a circle before the slightly more dramatic flaring of its bell (detail #5). The small diameter of the bell (detail #6) suggests that the French horn technique of hand-in bell was not utilized with this instrument. The instrument fits into a wood case painted black (details #7 and #8), possibly the same one it left the Gautrot factory in which it was manufactured in the 19th century.
Player - Instrument Interface and Sound Production
We have not found any images of this instrument being played but can surmise from wear marks on the instrument’s finish and by the positioning of its valves that its performer would have operated the valves with their right hand and held the coils of the instrument’s tubing with their left hand probably at a slight angle to vertical so that the downward-facing bell pointed to the performer’s left. Although the fundamental pitches (E1 – B-flat1) of this instrument when configures as a B-flat horn can be sounded, it is likely that it was generally sounded between its second and eighth partials, giving it a practical range of E2 to B-flat4. (when performed by professionals, this practical range could be extended at its top end by a few to several tones). It is fully chromatic over its entire range.
Origins/History/Evolution
The early 19th century invention of various kinds of valve mechanisms and Industrial Revolution advances in the mechanization of production led to an explosion in the number and types of brasswind instruments from the mid-19th century on. In an 1845 patent, Adolphe Sax attempted to incorporate the best design features of brasswind instruments of the day into a design that could be used throughout the entire range of brasswind instruments; he called the resulting instruments saxhorns. A number of other contemporary instrument makers emulated Sax’s ideas and instruments, resulting in many new instrument designs: 
“During the mid-19th century, numerous instruments in the medium register emerged, some with peculiar names and wraps. These demonstrate makers’ efforts to produce alternatives to the French horn, and might also show makers’ efforts to compete with Sax while his patents remained in force. Most of these instruments were circular, but few were essentially different from saxhorns (Herbert and Myers, p, 409).
Amongst these instrument makers was Pierre Gautrot, whose company designed and produced the saxhorn variant described above. We are not sure what Gautrot actually called this instrument, but it seems to us to be based on Sax’s tenor-range saxhorn baryton in B-flat with the following alterations: it uses Perinét valves instead of Berlin valves; it is circular in shape with a downward-facing bell instead of oval in shape with upward facing bell; and there is a greater length of cylindrical tubing prior to entering the instrument’s valve section and a shorter length of conical tuning after the valves than is the case with Sax’s saxhorn baryton. We have been unable to find out for how long Gautrot produced this model and if he had a particular market, such as military bands in certain countries, in mind for the instrument.

dcterms:title: matepe
dcterms:description:
Contextual Associations
The matepe is a plucked lamellaphone idiophone of Shona-speaking peoples (Kore-Kore, Budya, and Sena Tonga) of northeast Zimbabwe. Variants of it are also found in central Mozambique and southern Malawi. This matepe was made in 2020 by Boyi Nyamande of Nyamapanda/Nyampanda (a northeast Zimbabwe town on the Zimbabwe-Mozambique border). He performs matepe along with other family members for bira (ancestral rituals), the primary context in which this instrument is heard in northeast Zimbabwe.
Description
The wood soundboard (made from a soft wood) is hollowed out from the bottom sidewall of the board to a depth of approximately 4.5 inches to produce an integral resonating space (detail #1). This matepe has 26 narrow and flexible metal keys (longest key is 9 inches; shortest key is 4.5 inches), many of them at the middle of the keyboard curved upwards. The layout of these tongues is V-shaped with the longest and lowest-pitched keys in the center and the shorter and higher-pitched keys toward the sides (gallery #1). A length of wire is used to attach a metal pressure bar (details #2 and #3 for front and back views of the attachment method), which holds the instrument’s tongues in place. The bar’s downward pressure pushes the non-playing end of the tongues against the soundboard and the playing end against a thin metal bar (acting as a bridge; see detail #2) positioned on the top face of the soundboard. It is the length of each key that protrudes beyond the bridge that is plucked/sounded during performance. The instrument can be wedged inside a hemispheric gourd resonator (not shown) the rim of which is lined with devices that add a buzz to the primary sound of the instrument and amplifies it.
Player - Instrument Interface and Sound Production
Played either standing or seated, the sides of the resonator held between the palms of the player’s two hands. Keys sounded with the tips of the thumbs and index fingers of both hands (thumbs with a downward motion mostly on the longer, centrally located keys, the index fingers with an upward motion mostly on the shortest keys near the sides of the instrument). Tuned to a hexatonic (6-tone) scale.
Origins/History/Evolution
Because the matepe is associated with ancestral veneration religious practices and with peoples on the fringes of the Shona “supertribal” national umbrella, “… it remains largely outside of the Zimbabwean national imagination and outside of school, church and festival contexts” (Moon, p. 194). It therefore has not been researched and written about as much as some other Zimbabwean lamellaphone traditions. This does not mean that it does not have a long presence in what are now Zimbabwe and Mozambique, just that it has not become a focus of either indigenous or outside researchers on the music of this region. Field recordings of the matepe being played were made between the 1930s and 1970s by Hugh and Andrew Tracey and can be accessed through the International Library of African Music in South Africa; however, the instrument and its musical practice almost certainly go back in time much further than that. It is interesting to note that “since 2008, the online environment has helped to create virtual spaces where archival materials of matepe music are used by individuals to learn how to play the instrument” (Moon, p. 195). Moon (p.197) states that “After four years of researching matepe, I know of less than ten master musicians in Zimbabwe who play the instrument. I would estimate that there are upwards of thirty or forty players worldwide who are utilizing online resources to learn matepe, with still more who are actively engaged in watching and discussing video postings.” One such online resource is matepe.org.

dcterms:title: gong pulu
dcterms:subject: 111.222 idiophone—metallophone with one or more plaques suspended over a resonator
dcterms:description:
Contextual Associations
The gong pulu is a percussion plaque metallophone idiophone of the Balinese people of Indonesia. It is found today primarily in the gamelan gambuh--a small ensemble used to accompany the gambuh theatre—where it is used to punctuate the ends of melodic phrases. McGraw (2014) calls this instrument the kempur komodong/kemodong and says that it is used in smaller Balinese ensembles as a substitute for the medium-sized bronze gong kempur. He mentions its presence in gamelan pejogedan and gamelan paardjaan but does not mention its use in the gamelan gambuh.
Description
The two nearly-identical-in-size percussion keys of this gong pulu are made from iron covered with yellow-gold paint, probably to give them the appearance of being made from brass or bronze. These keys are suspended side-by-side over a hole cut in the top face of rectangular-box resonating space made of six wooden boards of differing dimensions that are nailed together. The keys are suspended from a single rope of plastic that is threaded through holes drilled into the sides of the resonator box (detail #1). As the two segments of this rope pass from side-to-side of the resonator, they run over metal supports located at their midpoints to assist in bearing the weight of the keys. Each key has two holes drilled into it each a quarter of the length of the key from each end and through which the suspension rope passes twice (detail #2); the small loop created by this on the underside of the keys has a small peg of wood through it (not visible in any of the images), keeping the rope from sliding back through the hole in the key. A seventh board of wood is carved decoratively and slides into grooves cut into the back of the resonator’s side boards (detail #1 and gallery #1 images). A V-shaped beater is used to strike the instrument’s two keys simultaneously. It is made from two standard gong beaters joined together at one end (detail #3).
Player - Instrument Interface and Sound Production
The player of the gong pulu sits cross-legged on the ground facing the instrument (as seen in gallery #1) and holding the beater in his/her right hand. The two keys of the instrument are tuned nearly identically to one another with just enough difference between them to create an acoustic beat when they are struck simultaneously. They typically produce the lowest pitch frequency in the ensemble in which they are found. Because the beater heads are thickly padded, the sound produced by striking the keys has a soft attack and relatively long sustain, which imitates quite closely the sound of the larger knobbed gongs found in other Balinese ensembles.
Origins/History/Evolution
No information on the history and origins of the gong pulu was found. There is a similar instrument (the gong kemodhong) found in a number of regional ensembles on the neighboring islands of Java and Madura, but we have not come across a definitive source saying that the instrument first existed on one island before being introduced to the others.
